about.family: We're a family business in the Netherlands, run by a husband and wife team.
about.story1: We've always loved travelling and the moments that make you stop—a view along the road, or a painting in a museum you'd only seen in books—and later wish you could keep that feeling around. That's a big part of why PrintMe exists.
about.story2: Our prints are made to bring that "good moment" onto your walls: clean, beautiful, and easy to live with. Whether it's a Dutch landscape, a Van Gogh, or your own photo, we hope it turns your house into a home.
about.intro1: We create museum-quality prints made to look stunning up close and stay beautiful for years: giclée on fine-art cotton paper, or a real photographic print with our Premium Poster.
about.intro2: Our collection brings together public-domain masterpieces from leading museums—Rembrandt, Vermeer, Van Gogh, Monet and many more—printed from the museums' own high-resolution files. We try to keep the feel of the original and bring it into your home.
about.intro3: Every print is produced with care, using premium materials and sharp, true-to-life color. Clean, timeless, and made to live with—so your walls feel more like you.
about.factsText: We're independent, and every day we carefully make prints that will bring you joy for years
about.imageAlt: Fashion designers collaborating in a bright studio
about.v1Text: Archival inks on premium paper. Made to last decades, not months. The kind of quality you'd expect in a gallery.
about.v2Text: Pick your size and paper, add a passe-partout and our Natural Oak frame if you like. Your art, your way—without the custom framing markup.
about.v3Text: Simple ordering, fast shipping, real humans if you need help. No hoops, no surprises, just smooth.
about.f1Text: Giclée on cotton paper, or a real photographic print
about.f2Text: Family-owned business led by two passionate engineers
about.f3Text: Choose from many sizes and papers, with an optional oak frame

how.intro: PrintMeArt is a family-run studio in Den Bosch. We make prints that are meant to look great in real homes: sharp up close, clean in the highlights, and rich in the shadows—without the "cheap poster" feel. This page explains what happens between your click and the moment it lands on your wall.
how.shortText: You choose the artwork (ours or yours), customize it (paper, size, frame), preview the result, and place the order. From there, we focus on getting the final print to look intentional: balanced framing, clean edges, and a consistent finish. If something doesn't meet our standard, it doesn't go out.
how.step1Text: You can shop from our curated collection, or bring your own image. If it's your own file, the goal is simple: make it look like it belongs on a wall, not just on a screen.
how.step2Text: Choose your paper type, select the size, and add a frame if you want a ready-to-hang result. The preview is there so you can see the overall look before you commit—especially important for cropping and borders.
how.step3Text: We don't just "hit print." We make sure the final result looks clean and premium: sensible cropping, neat alignment, and a finished presentation that works with your chosen frame and size.
how.step4Text: Your print is produced as a giclée on fine-art cotton paper, or as a photographic print on Premium Poster, for detail and smooth tone transitions. After printing, we check for the things you'd notice immediately: clean edges, consistent tones, and a tidy final result.
how.papersText: Museum-grade cotton papers from 308 to 350 g/m², fade-resistant and built to last. For everyday art there is our Premium Poster on photo paper.
how.photoRagText: Premium German fine art paper with natural white tone. Museum-grade archival quality used by galleries worldwide.
how.etchingText: Natural white cotton paper from Hahnemühle with a fine texture. Soft to the touch, with an artistic, painterly look.
how.barytaAlt: Hahnemühle FineArt Baryta paper up close
how.barytaText: Bright white, glossy baryta paper like classic darkroom paper. Gives the deepest blacks and the most contrast of all our papers.
how.canonText: Clean, neutral matte finish with high detail. Premium rag paper feel with a soft fine-art look. Ideal for color-critical photography.
how.posterSpec: 234 g/m² · Fujifilm photo paper · Fine matte
how.posterText: A real photographic print with vivid, true-to-life colours and deep blacks. The fine matte finish is glare-free and resists fingerprints. The best value for everyday art.
how.posterBest: Everyday art, a first artwork on the wall, budget-conscious
how.posterPrint: Exposed on Fujifilm Crystal Archive photo paper
how.notArchival: Not cotton paper; for museum grade, choose Photo Rag
how.chooseText: Think about your artwork and what matters most to you.
how.choose1Text: Soft, natural colors with a gallery feel. Smooth surface brings out fine details without distraction. Our most versatile choice.
how.choose2Text: Visible texture adds a hand-painted, tactile quality. Makes brushstrokes feel real. Great for classical art or expressive works.
how.choose3Text: Maximum color accuracy and deep blacks. Perfect tonal range from highlights to shadows. Ideal when precise color reproduction matters.
how.choose4Text: A real photographic print on matte Fujifilm paper. Vivid colours, no glare. Perfect for decorating without the premium price.
how.notSureText: Go with Photo Rag — it works beautifully for almost anything. All our cotton papers are museum-quality, fade-resistant and giclée printed with pigment inks.
how.framingText: Framing is optional, but it's the fastest way to make a print feel "done." It also adds everyday protection during handling and display. We offer one frame, chosen to suit almost any artwork:
how.careText: For the best longevity, avoid constant direct sunlight and keep prints away from high humidity spots. If you frame it, display behind glazing for extra protection and easier cleaning. Treat it like a good jacket: it'll last longer if you don't leave it in the rain.
how.faqPosterA: Only if you pick our Premium Poster, and even then not in the "thin paper, quick print" sense: it's a real photographic print on Fujifilm photo paper. Our cotton papers are fine-art giclée prints of museum quality.
how.faqOwn: Can I print my own photo or artwork?
how.faqOwnA: Yes. Upload your file, customize the size/paper/frame, preview it, and order. If you want it to feel truly premium, pick a size that matches your image well instead of forcing extreme cropping.
how.faqMatteA: For colour-critical photos, choose Hahnemühle Photo Rag: smooth cotton with fine detail. Premium Poster is a real photographic print with vivid colours and deep blacks, at the best price.
how.faqShippingA: Orders are delivered within {{days}} days. We always use tracked shipping so you know when to expect it.

intro.Art Prints: Paintings, watercolours, drawings and prints from five centuries, all old enough to be in the public domain and photographed by the museums that own them. We start from the museum's own high-resolution file, check colour and detail, and print each work as a giclée on the fine-art paper you choose, in our studio in Den Bosch. The collection is grouped by subject: landscapes, seascapes, cities, portraits, still lifes, flowers, animals and early abstract art. Most of it comes from the Rijksmuseum, the Art Institute of Chicago, the National Gallery of Art in Washington and Birmingham Museums, and every print can be framed to order.
intro.Still Life: In the 17th century Dutch and Flemish painters turned flowers, fruit, glassware and food into a genre of their own. Their bouquets were often imaginary: tulips, roses and irises that never bloomed in the same week, painted from separate studies, sometimes with a fly or a snail as a reminder that beauty fades. Jan Davidsz. de Heem, Balthasar van der Ast and Jan van Huysum represent that tradition here. Later painters kept returning to it, from Claude Monet's Spring Flowers (1864) and Van Gogh's Irises to Odilon Redon's dreamy flower pieces and the American John Frederick Peto, whose everyday objects look real enough to pick up.
intro.Animal Art: Animals have their own place in art history, from the exotic birds painted for wealthy collectors to the cats of Paris. In this group you will find Jan Asselijn's The Threatened Swan, the first painting ever bought for the Rijksmuseum's predecessor in 1800, and Melchior d'Hondecoeter's birds near a pool, by the 17th-century specialist in poultry and parkland birds. Aert Schouman's watercolours of birds, a monkey among fruit by Jean-Baptiste Oudry, Théophile-Alexandre Steinlen's cats from 1909 and Toyohara Chikanobu's leaping carp add variety in time and style. Many of these prints work well in a child's room, a study or a country kitchen.
intro.Botanical Art: Flowers have been painted for science and for pleasure, and this group holds both. The 17th-century Dutch flower piece is at its core, with arrangements by Jan Davidsz. de Heem, Balthasar van der Ast, Jacob Marrel and Jan van Huysum that show tulips, roses and fritillaries in precise detail. Botanical plates add the scientific side, such as a study of a passion flower and a wild rose. From the 19th century come Claude Monet's Spring Flowers, Van Gogh's Irises, painted in May 1890 just before he left the asylum in Saint-Rémy, and the softly coloured vases of Odilon Redon. Flowers on paper also brighten a room when the garden is bare.
intro.Landscape: Landscape is the largest group in our catalog, and for good reason: for centuries painters went outside to record fields, rivers, woods and skies, and those views still give a room space and calm. It spans the Dutch 17th century, with Hendrick Avercamp's frozen rivers, Aert van der Neer's moonlight and Salomon van Ruysdael's dunes, and the 19th century of the Barbizon painters, the Hague School and the Impressionists. Alfred Sisley's villages along the Seine and Vincent van Gogh's wheat fields and olive groves are among the best-loved prints here, alongside English watercolours, American scenes by George Inness and Winslow Homer, and Hokusai's views of Mount Fuji.
intro.Abstract Art: Abstract painting is younger than most people think. Only around 1910 did a few artists dare to leave out the visible world altogether, and Wassily Kandinsky was among the very first. His Painting with Troika (1911) still hides three horses and a sleigh among its colours; two years later, in Painting with Green Center, hardly any recognisable shape remains. This small group follows that moment, with Alexej von Jawlensky's Frosty Day (1915) and Louis Marcoussis's Cubist The Musician (1914) from the National Gallery of Art. Strong colour and clear shapes make these prints a natural fit for modern interiors and plain white walls.
intro.Portraits: A good portrait is about more than a likeness: it shows how someone wanted to be seen, or how the painter saw them. Our portraits range from Joshua Reynolds and Henry Raeburn, painting the British gentry around 1800, to the Impressionists' friends and family. Édouard Manet painted his fellow artist Berthe Morisot with a muff around 1868, Renoir the young Romaine Lacaux in 1864, and Van Gogh in 1888 the Arles girl he called La Mousmé, after a Japanese word he had found in a novel. Portraits by Modigliani, William Merritt Chase and Robert Henri bring the group into the 20th century.
intro.Seascapes: For a seafaring country like the Dutch Republic, ships were a matter of pride, and painters such as Willem van de Velde the Younger and Ludolf Bakhuizen made sea battles and storms their speciality. The Battle of Scheveningen of 1653 by Jan Abrahamsz Beerstraaten belongs to that tradition. In the 19th century the coast became a place of leisure and light: Eugène Boudin painted the beaches and harbours of Trouville, Deauville and Le Havre, Winslow Homer the fishing villages of England and New England, and J. M. W. Turner fishing boats caught in a squall. Seascapes open up a wall like a window onto the horizon.
intro.Cityscapes & Architecture: Cities have been painted with the same care as landscapes, and the results are often a record of streets and buildings that have since changed or disappeared. Pieter Saenredam painted Amsterdam's old town hall in 1657, five years after it burned down, from drawings he had made in 1641, and Vermeer's The Little Street shows a real house in Delft. From the 19th century come Thomas Shotter Boys's hand-coloured lithographs of London and Paris, views of Venice by Canaletto's followers, Alfred Sisley's Argenteuil and Ernest Lawson's Flatiron Building in New York. Cityscapes suit a hallway or study, where there is time to look at the details.
intro.Famous Painters: Some visitors look for a subject, others for a name. This part of the shop is arranged by painter and period instead: the Renaissance of Bruegel and Cranach, the Dutch masters from Avercamp and Vermeer to the Hague School, the Romantics and Realists of the 19th century, and the modern masters, from Monet and Van Gogh to Kandinsky. Each group gathers the works we print by the leading artists of that time, with the museum and date of the original on every product page. It is a good place to start if you already know whose work you would like on your wall.
intro.Renaissance Masters: North of the Alps the Renaissance of the 15th and 16th centuries had its own character: less interested in ideal bodies than in landscape, daily life and minute detail. Pieter Bruegel the Elder brought those together in Hunters in the Snow (1565), where tired hunters return to a village in the snow while skaters play on the ice below. Lucas Cranach the Elder, court painter to the Electors of Saxony, painted a princely hunt near Hartenfels Castle in Torgau in 1540. The panels by the Master of the St Elizabeth Panels show the St Elizabeth's Flood of 1421, which swallowed the Grote Waard near Dordrecht and gave rise to today's Biesbosch.
intro.Dutch Masters: Painting in the Northern Netherlands had two golden moments, and this group covers both. In the 17th century, the Golden Age, painters specialised in winter scenes, seascapes, still lifes and cities: Hendrick Avercamp's skaters, Aert van der Neer's moonlight, Willem van de Velde's ships and Vermeer's The Little Street in Delft. Two centuries later Vincent van Gogh, born in Zundert in North Brabant, began as a painter of peasants and weavers before his years in France, and the Hague School painted the polders under grey skies. Many of these originals hang in the Rijksmuseum and the Mauritshuis; here they come home in print.
intro.Modern Masters: Between the 1870s and the First World War painting changed more than in the three centuries before. The Impressionists broke up colour into quick strokes of light; Van Gogh, Cézanne and Toulouse-Lautrec made colour and line carry emotion and structure; and by 1911 Kandinsky had painted almost without subject at all. This group follows that path with Claude Monet, Camille Pissarro and Renoir, Van Gogh's work from Arles and Saint-Rémy, Cézanne's Boy in a Red Vest, Paul Signac's harbour views, Modigliani's portraits and Kandinsky's Painting with Troika. These are the painters who still define what many people mean by modern art.
intro.Romantic & Realist Masters: The 19th century had two great moods. Romanticism looked for feeling and the sublime: J. M. W. Turner painting the burning Houses of Parliament in 1834, Thomas Cole's views of Florence and New England, storms and mountain lakes. Realism, from the 1850s, preferred the world as it was: Jean-François Millet's peasants, Winslow Homer's fishermen and the quiet polder views of the Hague School. This group brings together leading names of both, along with the English watercolourists, from David Cox to Thomas Shotter Boys, whose views of towns and countryside sit somewhere in between. A good place to look for drama, or for an honest everyday scene.

faq.resolutionQ: How sharp does my photo need to be?
faq.resolutionA: For a sharp print we want at least 200 pixels per inch at the size you choose. When you upload, you see the print quality for every size straight away. If your image falls short, we switch on professional upscaling (€5): we enlarge and sharpen your image before printing. You can turn it off yourself.
faq.filesA: PNG, JPG or GIF, up to 150 MB. A photo straight from your phone or camera works fine; the bigger the original, the larger you can print it.
faq.processA: We look at every file ourselves: the crop, the alignment and the white border. If your image needs a different crop to fit, we send you the final design to approve first, so you have the last word. Then we print it, check edges and colours, and pack it rolled up in a protective tube.
faq.paperA: For photos where colour really matters, choose Hahnemühle Photo Rag: smooth cotton paper with fine detail, printed as a giclée with pigment inks and fade-resistant for over 100 years.
